title: Raga Malar
hookLine: the monsoon raga opens not with rain but with what everyone forgets

lines: THE FIRST DROPS ON A DRY STREET.
cards: The first fat drops hit the dry street, and the smell changes before anything else does. Then the sky opens. People who were walking start running.
Someone pulls laundry off a line. A child stands in the yard with her face up and her mouth open. For a few minutes, everyone stops and looks up.
Rain does that. The Guru Granth Sahib has a raga that tradition gives to the rainy season, called Malar. And its first hymn makes everyone look up, without a drop of rain in it.

teach.h: AFTER SARANG: THE RAINS BREAK THE HEAT.
teach.b: Malar follows Sarang in the Granth's order, so the book moves from the heat of midday to the rains that break it. Tradition calls Malar the monsoon raga and sings it in the rainy season.
Its pages are full of rain pictures: clouds, thunder, the bird that cries out for a single drop. But here's the surprise. The section opens with a hymn of Guru Nanak that isn't about rain at all.
In paraphrase: eating, drinking, laughing, sleeping, we have forgotten dying. Forgetting the Master, we've brought ourselves to ruin; a life like that won't last.
Then the turn: meditate on the one Name, and go home with your honor.

A hard first line for a rain song? Think back to the street. Eating, drinking, laughing, sleeping: that's the ordinary loop, and it's fine, until it runs so smoothly that a person forgets where it ends.

Then the rain comes, the loop breaks for a few minutes, and everyone looks up. Malar's opening does the same thing in words. It interrupts, just long enough to ask what the routine has made you forget.
And rain in a hot country isn't gloomy. It's relief, what lets the fields live.
Guru Nanak's interruption comes the same way: a hard word about a life that won't last, and then relief, the one Name, and the way home with honor. Today's line: rain.

how: In kirtan, shabads from the Malar section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in Raga Malar, which tradition associates with the monsoon and sings in the rainy season.

games.why: the hymn interrupts the ordinary loop, the way rain does, and turns to the one Name and going home with honor.

practice: If it's raining, open a window a little and listen, or play a shabad sung in Malar; if not, sit in the quiet and let this minute be the interruption: no eating, no scrolling, no planning, just slow breath.

Look up, at the ceiling or the sky, and let one honest thought come about where your days are going, without arguing with it. If you pray, hold Guru Nanak's line about the one Name; if you don't, simply look up.

wordCard.voice: Raga Malar. The monsoon raga that follows Sarang, sung by tradition in the rains, opening with Guru Nanak's line that in eating, drinking, laughing and sleeping we have forgotten dying. Today's word.
